{{short description|Texas Instruments' response to a project to factorize cryptographic keys}}
{{Primary sources|date=September 2021}}
[[Image:Ti83plus.jpg|right|200px|thumb|A TI-83+ graphing calculator displaying a [[sine wave]]]]
The '''Texas Instruments signing key controversy''' resulted from [[Texas Instruments]]' (TI) response to a project to [[RSA problem|factorize]] the 512-[[bit]] [[RSA (cryptosystem)|RSA]] [[key (cryptography)|cryptographic keys]] needed to write custom [[firmware]] to TI devices.

==Project==
In July 2009, Benjamin Moody, a United-TI [[Internet forum|forum]] user, published the [[integer factorization|factors]] of a 512-bit [[RSA (cryptosystem)|RSA]] key used to sign the [[TI-83 series|TI-83+ series]] graphing calculator. The discovery of the private key would allow end users to [[flash memory|flash]] their own [[operating system]]s onto the device without having to use any special hardware. Moody used two [[free software]] implementations of the [[general number field sieve]], msieve and ggnfs; the computation took 73 days on a 1.9&nbsp;GHz dual-core processor. This demonstrates the progress of hardware development: the factorization of the similar 512-bit [[RSA-155]] in 1999 using the same algorithm required a large dedicated research group, 8000 MIPS-years of computing time, and a [[Cray C90|Cray C916]] supercomputer.<ref>Herman te Riele (1999-08-26), [https://listserv.nodak.edu/cgi-bin/wa.exe?A2=NMBRTHRY;89b68928.9908 New factorization record] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624195723/https://listserv.nodak.edu/cgi-bin/wa.exe?A2=NMBRTHRY;89b68928.9908 |date=2021-06-24 }} (announcement of factorization of RSA-155). Retrieved on 2008-03-10.</ref>

In response, members of the wider TI graphing calculators community (at yAronet) set up a [[BOINC]]-based [[distributed computing]] project, RSA Lattice Siever (RSALS for short), that quickly factored the other keys.<ref>
{{cite web
|url=http://www.ticalc.org/archives/news/articles/14/145/145273.html
|title=All TI Signing Keys Factored&nbsp;— ticalc.org
|publisher=www.ticalc.org
|access-date=2009-09-21
}}
</ref>
RSA Lattice Siever remained active for nearly three years after outliving its initial purpose, by factoring other integers for the mathematical community.
After factoring over 400 integers,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://boinc.unsads.com/rsals/crunching.php|title=NumbersRSALS Does not run anymore - Homepage - NFS@Home|date=October 14, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121014185408/http://boinc.unsads.com/rsals/crunching.php |archive-date=2012-10-14 }}</ref> RSALS moved to RSALS-inspired NFS@home<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mersenneforum.org/showpost.php?p=306539&postcount=434|title=mersenneforum.org - View Single Post - BOINC NFS sieving - RSALS|website=www.mersenneforum.org|access-date=2022-11-15|archive-date=2022-11-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221115050557/https://www.mersenneforum.org/showpost.php?p=306539&postcount=434|url-status=live}}</ref> at the end of August 2012.

==Legal response==
Texas Instruments began by sending out two initial [[Digital Millennium Copyright Act]] (DMCA) take-down requests to the hackers, referring to sites or forum posts that they controlled.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://brandonw.net/calcstuff/DMCA_notice.txt |title=brandonw.net |publisher=brandonw.net |access-date=2010-05-24 |archive-date=2024-07-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701184439/https://brandonw.net/calcstuff/DMCA_notice.txt |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web
|url=http://www.ticalc.org/archives/news/articles/14/145/145316.html
|title=Signing Keys and the DMCA&nbsp;— ticalc.org
|publisher=www.ticalc.org
|access-date=2009-09-21
|archive-date=2024-07-01
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701184445/https://www.ticalc.org/archives/news/articles/14/145/145316.html
|url-status=live
}}</ref> The hackers responded by removing the keys, without consulting an attorney.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theregister.co.uk/2009/09/23/texas_instruments_calculator_hacking/ |title=Texas Instruments aims lawyers at calculator hackers |publisher=The Register |date=2009-09-23 |access-date=2011-01-01 |archive-date=2011-01-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110101000327/http://www.theregister.co.uk/2009/09/23/texas_instruments_calculator_hacking/ |url-status=live }}</ref> TI then sent further DMCA notices to a variety<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2009/09/ti-leave-those-kids-alone |title=UPDATE: Hey, TI, Leave Those Kids Alone &#124; Electronic Frontier Foundation |publisher=Eff.org |date=2009-09-25 |access-date=2010-05-24 |archive-date=2024-07-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701184434/https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2009/09/ti-leave-those-kids-alone |url-status=live }}</ref> of [[website]]s displaying the keys, including United-TI, [[Reddit]], and [[Wikipedia]].<ref>{{cite web
| url         = https://wikimediafoundation.org/wiki/DMCA_Texas_Instruments
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20111125220545/http://wikimediafoundation.org/wiki/DMCA_Texas_Instruments
| url-status  = dead
| archive-date = November 25, 2011
| title       = DMCA Texas Instruments
| access-date  = 2014-02-03
| date        = 2009-09-25
}}</ref> Texas Instruments' efforts then became subject to the [[Streisand effect]],<ref>{{cite web
|url=http://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2009/09/texas_instrumen.html
|title=Schneier on Security: Texas Instruments Signing Keys Broken
|publisher=www.schneier.com
|access-date=2009-10-06
|archive-date=2009-09-28
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090928090251/http://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2009/09/texas_instrumen.html
|url-status=live
}}</ref> and the keys were mirrored on a number of sites, including [[WikiLeaks]].<ref>[https://wikileaks.org/wiki/Suppressed_Texas_Instruments_cryptographic_signing_keys,_28_Aug_2009 Suppressed Texas Instruments cryptographic signing keys, 28 Aug 2009] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100606104835/https://wikileaks.org/wiki/Suppressed_Texas_Instruments_cryptographic_signing_keys,_28_Aug_2009 |date=6 June 2010 }}at [[WikiLeaks]]. on 10 April 2012.</ref> In September 2009, Dan Goodin from ''[[The Register]]'' alerted the [[Electronic Frontier Foundation]] (EFF) to TI's actions, and the EFF agreed to take on the case ''[[pro bono]]'', representing three people who had received DMCA notices.

On October 13, 2009, the EFF sent a letter to TI warning them that the posting of the keys did not violate the DMCA, and that it might be liable for [[misrepresentation]].<ref>{{cite web
|url=https://www.eff.org/press/archives/2009/10/13
|title=EFF Warns Texas Instruments to Stop Harassing Calculator Hobbyists
|date=13 October 2009
|publisher=EFF official press release
|access-date=2009-10-25
|archive-date=2009-10-17
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091017110759/http://www.eff.org/press/archives/2009/10/13
|url-status=live
}}</ref> Despite the letter by the EFF, TI continued to send DMCA notices to websites that posted the keys, but stopped doing so after late 2009. The EFF filed a [[DMCA 512|DMCA Section 512 counter-notice]] on behalf of three of the bloggers who received DMCA notices. When the EFF did not receive a response by the deadline, the bloggers reposted the content that had been taken down.<ref>{{cite web
|url=https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2009/10/texas-instruments-stop-digging-holes
|date=October 29, 2009
|title=Hey, Texas Instruments -- Stop Digging Holes
|publisher=EFF Deeplinks Blog
|access-date=2009-10-29
|last=Granick
|first=Jennifer
|archive-date=2024-07-01
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701184435/https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2009/10/texas-instruments-stop-digging-holes
|url-status=live
}}</ref>

==Cryptographic keys==
The public (or verifying) [[RSA (cryptosystem)|RSA]] parameters of the original [[TI-83+]] / TI-83+ Silver Edition OS signing key factored by Benjamin Moody are the following 512-bit modulus ''n'' and exponent ''e'' (specified in [[hexadecimal]]):<ref>{{cite web|url=http://wlstorage.net/file/ti-os-keys-dmca-2009.txt
|title=File |publisher=WikiLeaks |access-date=2012-04-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120314170835/http://wlstorage.net/file/ti-os-keys-dmca-2009.txt |archive-date=2012-03-14 |url-status=usurped}}
</ref>

 n = 82EF4009ED7CAC2A5EE12B5F8E8AD9A0AB9CC9F4F3E44B7E8BF2D57A2F2BEACE83424E1CFF0D2A5A7E2E53CB926D61F347DFAA4B35B205B5881CEB40B328E58F
 e = 11

By factoring ''n'', Moody obtained the factors ''p'' (252 bits) and ''q'' (260 bits), which can be used in turn to quickly compute the 512-bit private (or [[Digital Signature|signing]]) key <math>d=e^{-1} \bmod (p-1)(q-1)</math>:

 p = B709D3A0CD2FEC08EAFCCF540D8A100BB38E5E091D646ADB7B14D021096FFCD
 q = B7207BD184E0B5A0B89832AA68849B29EDFB03FBA2E8917B176504F08A96246CB
 d = 4D0534BA8BB2BFA0740BFB6562E843C7EC7A58AE351CE11D43438CA239DD99276CD125FEBAEE5D2696579FA3A3958FF4FC54C685EAA91723BC8888F292947BA1

The value ''d'' can then be used to sign arbitrary OS software.

The keys factored by RSA Lattice Siever (the [[TI-92 series#TI-92 Plus|TI-92+]], [[TI-73]], [[TI-89]], [[TI-92 series#Voyage 200|Voyage 200]], [[TI-89]] Titanium, [[TI-84+]] / TI-84 Silver Edition OS signing and date-stamp signing keys) are similar but with different values of ''n'', ''p'', ''q'', and ''d''. A single date-stamp signing key is shared by all models.
